old: In Hungarian, spatial movement often uses postpositions: *keresztül* (through, across), *felé* (towards), and *felől* (from the direction of). Unlike English prepositions, they stand after the noun (which is in the nominative case, or takes a superessive case with *keresztül* / *át*).
new: You know *keresztül* (through, across) with *-n / -on / -en / -ön* from A2 (Unit 5). New here are *felé* (towards) and *felől* (from the direction of). Like all postpositions they stand after the noun; *felé* and *felől* take the plain nominative: *a város felé*, *a hegyek felől*.
why: Screen presents keresztül as new (A2 Unit 5, keresztul) and does not say which case felé/felől take.

old: Key verbal compounds include *átszáll vmire* (to change onto something, taking the sublative *-ra / -re*) and *menetrend szerint* (according to timetable).
new: You know verbs that govern *-ra / -re* from Unit 3: *átszáll vmire* (to change onto something) works the same way. Another useful phrase is *menetrend szerint* (according to the timetable).
why: Recap -ra/-re government (B1 Unit 3, verb-government-ra-re).

old: Hungarian verbal prefixes modify motion verbs: *átkel* (to cross over), *átmegy* (to go across), *beér* (to arrive in/reach), and *felmegy* (to go up). When followed by *keresztül* or *-on / -en / -ön át*, they describe crossing terrain like rivers, passes, and tunnels.
new: You know directional prefixes such as *fel-*, *le-*, *be-* from A1 (Unit 28) and *keresztül* from A2 (Unit 5). Now *át-* joins them: *átkel* (to cross over), *átmegy* (to go across); *beér* (to arrive in) and *felmegy* (to go up) work the same way. With *keresztül* or *-on / -en / -ön át* they describe crossing rivers, passes and tunnels.
why: Screen presents the directional prefixes fel-/le-/be- (A1 Unit 28) and keresztül (A2 Unit 5) as new.
Right option 13 vs 9 chars.
